stems.text: Your hyaluronic-acid serum and dermal filler share a name, but they do completely different jobs.
The kind your body makes, the kind in your serum, and the kind a doctor injects.
And the mix-up is expensive. People buy a serum expecting the results of an injection, then wonder why nothing changed. A serum is not filler in a bottle.
Here's where the two versions really split — one stays a loose, flowing molecule. The other gets locked into a rigid mesh.
In a serum, size decides almost everything. Large chains mostly stay near the surface, forming a hydrating film. Smaller ones may travel farther into the upper layers of skin.
So why does the bottle say plumping? Hydrated surface cells can temporarily make fine lines appear softer — that's hydration, not correction.

Here's the part the marketing skips. Hyaluronic acid binds water — it doesn't manufacture it. Think of it as a sponge, not a water factory. A complete formula still needs something else — an ingredient that seals that water in, so it doesn't evaporate away.
A filler is chemically different. Its chains are cross-linked into a gel that holds its own shape, once it's placed beneath the skin, where it can physically add volume.
The name goes back to nineteen thirty-four, when it was isolated from the clear jelly inside a cow's eye.
Is a filler just serum with a needle? Not even close. Do not inject yourself.
That's the F D A's own wording, not ours. Dermal fillers are a medical procedure with real risks, including tissue death, vision loss and stroke. Choose a provider trained to perform the injection.

Same ingredient family — different size, different structure, different location. The body's version is a resident, the serum's version is hydration, the filler's version is volume. Serum hydrates, filler adds volume — same name, different jobs.
